newsitem.title: TURKEY: Mild optimism in Iraqi Kurd peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Mild optimism in Iraqi Kurd peace talks.

text.p: Rival Iraqi Kurdish groups begun the second day of U.S.-brokered peace talks in Turkey on Thursday amid mild optimism that the two feuding parties could shore up a week-old ceasefire agreement.
"Talks were quite well yesterday, but there were still some differences," a participant diplomat told Reuters.
U.S. envoy Robert Pelletreau, British and Turkish diplomats are overseeing the negotiations between the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK).
A Turkish foreign ministry official said the talks, criticised by Baghdad, were expected to end late on Thursday afternoon.
Pelletreau brokered a ceasefire between the Kurds last week after two months of clashes that gave President Saddam Hussein a foothold in northern Iraq after a five-year break.
Mediators say they are trying to strengthen the ceasefire before moving onto the key issues of control of the city of Arbil and the sharing of revenues from a KDP oil trade on the Turkish border.
Barzani joined forces with Baghdad in late August to take Arbil from the PUK, prompting U.S. missile strikes against targets in southern Iraq.
The KDP accuses Iran of backing the PUK militarily. Both Talabani and Tehran deny this.
The Iraqi Kurds broke from Baghdad with Western encouragement after Iraq's defeat in the 1991 Gulf War but the fighting has rendered a power-sharing regional parliament obsolete.
